name: Battles of Lexington and Concord
info: British regulars sent from Boston to seize military supplies at Concord fought Massachusetts militia at Lexington, Concord and along the road back on 19 April 1775, the first major fighting of the American Revolutionary War.

facts.date: 19 April 1775, from sunrise at Lexington until dusk at Charlestown
facts.place: Middlesex County in the Province of Massachusetts Bay, in the towns of Lexington, Concord, Lincoln, Menotomy (present-day Arlington) and Cambridge, along a road of about 17 miles (27 km) from Cambridge to Concord, in the present-day United States
facts.sides: British Army regulars from Boston, about 700 under Lieutenant Colonel Francis Smith with Major John Pitcairn, joined at Lexington by a brigade of about 1,000 under Brigadier General Earl Percy, about 1,700 in all; Massachusetts militia and minutemen, some 4,000 over the day, turning out piecemeal, with Brigadier General William Heath taking command of a phase of the fighting toward the day's end
facts.outcome: The British searched Concord and found few supplies, then returned to Boston under heavy fire with heavy losses and reached Charlestown at dusk. The militia then blockaded the land approaches, which began the siege of Boston.

t: The British expedition of about 700 men set out to seize colonial military supplies at Concord, but Patriot leaders had been warned weeks earlier and had moved most of them, so few weapons were taken and the march set off the fighting it was meant to prevent.

Who fired the first shot at Lexington is still uncertain: witnesses on each side blamed the other, many did not know, and David Hackett Fischer wrote that a shot was fired by an unknown person after both commanders had ordered their men to hold fire.

On the road back to Boston the British were attacked all day by militia who often fired from cover and from long range, and about half the day's fatalities on each side occurred at Menotomy and Cambridge.
dyk: The riders who warned the countryside set off a system of 'alarm and muster' that used bells, drums, alarm guns, bonfires and a trumpet, and people in towns 25 miles (40 km) from Boston knew of the British movements while the troops were still unloading their boats in Cambridge.
ev: Parliament passes the Coercive Acts and colonial leaders respond with the Suffolk Resolves and a Massachusetts Provincial Congress
Parliament declares Massachusetts to be in a state of rebellion
About 700 regulars are ferried across to Cambridge at night, and Paul Revere, William Dawes and Samuel Prescott ride to warn the countryside
Regulars and militia exchange fire at Lexington, where eight militiamen are killed
Militia force the British companies back across the Old North Bridge at Concord
The British retreat under fire and are reinforced by Percy's brigade at Lexington, then reach Charlestown at dusk
Militia from across New England surround Boston, beginning the siege

sections.background:
The British Army occupied Boston in 1768. After the Boston Tea Party of 1773, Parliament passed the Coercive Acts of 1774, which historians later renamed the Intolerable Acts. In the summer of 1774 colonial leaders in Suffolk County adopted the Suffolk Resolves, which declared the acts unconstitutional, recommended sanctions against Britain and urged Massachusetts residents to form their own government and fight in its defence. The First Continental Congress endorsed the Resolves on 17 September 1774, and the colonists formed the Massachusetts Provincial Congress. In February 1775 both houses of Parliament declared that a state of rebellion existed in the province.

General Thomas Gage, military governor of Massachusetts, commanded roughly 3,000 British troops in Boston and had lost control of the colony outside the town. He planned to avoid open conflict by taking military supplies from the militias through small, secret and rapid strikes. In one such strike the British seized supplies, but the Patriots hid the stores from other searches in nearly bloodless events known as the Powder Alarms. On 14 April 1775 Gage received instructions from the Earl of Dartmouth to disarm the rebels and imprison their leaders. He decided against written orders for the arrest of leaders, fearing that might spark an uprising. The militias had gathered weapons, powder and supplies at Concord and at Worcester, and Patriot leaders learned weeks before the expedition that the stores might be at risk and moved most of them.
sections.forces:
About 700 regulars, drawn from 11 of Gage's 13 infantry regiments in Boston, were put under the overall command of Lieutenant Colonel Francis Smith. Major John Pitcairn of the Marines commanded ten light infantry companies and Lieutenant Colonel Benjamin Bernard 11 grenadier companies. The force included 350 grenadiers and about 320 light infantry. Most of the captains were volunteers from all the regiments in Boston, attached to the companies at random, and the lack of familiarity between commanders and companies would cause communication and disciplinary problems. A second force, the 1st Brigade under Brigadier General Hugh Percy, about 1,000 strong with two 6-pounder guns, would follow later in the morning.

Under New England law every town had to form a militia company of all males of 16 and over, properly armed, and the companies elected their own officers. The total colonial force over the day included some 4,000 militiamen from local militia and minuteman companies, from thirty towns. The Provincial Congress had organised the companies into regiments and brigades, but units turned out piecemeal and several provincial generals were not in a position to assert overall command. At Lexington about 80 men of the town's training band, which was not a minuteman company, stood under Captain John Parker, a veteran of the French and Indian War.
sections.course:
The regulars crossed to Cambridge on the night of 18 April and began their 17-mile (27 km) march at about 2 am. At sunrise on 19 April, as Pitcairn's advance guard entered Lexington, Parker's men stood in ranks on the Common, not blocking the road. Parker ordered them to disperse and not fire, but a shot was fired and the regulars charged with bayonets. Eight militiamen were killed and ten wounded, while one British soldier was wounded. Order was restored by Smith and the column marched on to Concord.

At Concord Smith split his force to search for supplies. About 100 light infantry in seven companies held the North Bridge, and four companies went on to Barrett's Farm. At about 11:00 am at least 400 militiamen advanced on the 90 to 95 men guarding the bridge. A shot rang out, the British fired a ragged volley, and two Acton minutemen were killed. Major Buttrick then ordered the militia to fire, and the British fled. The regulars left Concord after noon.

On the march back more militia arrived and fired from cover, notably at Meriam's Corner, Brooks Hill and the Bloody Angle. Smith was wounded in the thigh and Pitcairn thrown from his horse. At about 2:30 pm Percy's brigade met the column at Lexington, and the combined force of about 1,700 set out again at 3:30 pm. The fighting was heaviest at Menotomy and Cambridge. Percy turned off towards Charlestown and the British reached it near dark.
sections.aftermath:
At Meriam's Corner two regulars were killed and perhaps six wounded, with no colonial casualties. At two sharp bends further on the British lost thirty killed or wounded and four militiamen were killed, three of them officers. At the North Bridge at least three privates of the 4th were killed or mortally wounded and nine more wounded. At the Jason Russell farm in Menotomy twenty-one colonial combatants and an unknown number of regulars died. At Menotomy and Cambridge the colonists lost 25 killed and nine wounded and the British 40 killed and 80 wounded, about half the day's fatalities for each side.

Exhausted and enraged troops were hard to control in the houses along the road. A few regulars committed atrocities, such as killing two drunk men at Cooper's Tavern. Taverns were ransacked and houses plundered, though colonists later exaggerated accounts of ransacking and burning, in part to gain compensation.

By the next morning Boston was surrounded by a militia army of over 15,000 men from New England, forming a siege line from Chelsea to Roxbury. The Second Continental Congress adopted these men into the beginnings of the Continental Army. Gage refused to impose martial law and persuaded the selectmen to surrender private weapons in return for permission for inhabitants to leave. The Provincial Congress sent sworn depositions to London, where newspapers printed them two weeks before Gage's report arrived. In London, politicians tended to blame Gage rather than their own policies.
sections.sources:
The accounts of the first shot at Lexington conflict. Lieutenant John Barker of the 4th Foot wrote that the militia fired two shots at his regiment. Captain Parker testified in a sworn deposition that the regulars rushed the militia and fired without provocation, and 34 militiamen deposed that nobody in their company fired before they were fired on. The Massachusetts Provincial Congress collected scores of sworn testimonies from militiamen and British prisoners within four days of the battle, and unfavourable depositions were not published and were returned to the participants, Paul Revere among them. Isaiah Thomas recalled Parker's words many years later, and older participants in later life all said the British fired first, though many had said at the time that they were unsure.

Modern historians differ in detail. Fischer wrote that both Pitcairn and Parker ordered their men to hold fire and that a shot came from an unknown person, possibly several near-simultaneous shots. Mark Urban wrote that one or two villagers opened fire and a British company then fired a volley without orders from Pitcairn. At the North Bridge, Captain Walter Laurie's later report called the first shot a warning shot by a panicked British soldier. Whether Margaret Gage was the source of the colonists' advance knowledge of the date is described only as reasonable speculation. Colonel Timothy Pickering was accused of letting the British pass at Winter Hill to avoid war, but he said he acted on Heath's orders, which Heath denied.
sections.legacy:
The expedition was a failure, since the battles caused the fighting it was meant to prevent and few weapons were seized. Parliament's George Germain, no friend of the colonists, wrote that the Bostonians were right to make the King's troops the aggressors. John Adams, who rode along the battlefields the next day, became convinced that the die was cast. Thomas Paine rejected England's 'hardened, sullen-tempered Pharaoh' after the news, and George Washington wrote that America would be either drenched in blood or inhabited by slaves.

It mattered to the early American government to maintain an image of British fault and American innocence, and paintings showed the Lexington fight as an unjustified slaughter. Early in the nineteenth century the dispute over the first shot grew and the battle took on an almost mythical quality, so that later paintings showed the militia standing and fighting back. Ralph Waldo Emerson's 'Concord Hymn' of 1837 helped Americans learn about the Revolution, and Longfellow's 'Paul Revere's Ride' was memorised by generations of schoolchildren after 1860, though it is historically inaccurate and Revere never reached Concord.

The Lexington Battle Green is a National Historic Landmark, and Minute Man National Historical Park holds the North Bridge and about 5 miles (8 km) of the road. Patriots' Day is a legal holiday in Massachusetts, observed on the third Monday in April, and on 19 April 1875 President Ulysses S. Grant joined 50,000 people at the centenary.

summary: On 19 April 1775 about 700 British regulars sent from Boston to seize supplies at Concord fought Massachusetts militia at Lexington, at Concord's North Bridge and along the road back. The militia then besieged Boston, and the fighting is counted the first major action of the American Revolutionary War.

notes: The article gives no total casualties for the day; only Lexington, the North Bridge, Meriam's Corner, the two bends, the Russell farm and Menotomy-Cambridge figures. I added nothing up.
The lead says approximately 400 militiamen and 100 regulars at the North Bridge; the body says at least 400 and 90-95. I used the body.
The article says Artemas Ward 'arrived on June 20', which is plainly wrong for a siege that began in April; left out.
The article says Regulars numbered about 700 but the militia alarm told of 'over 500'; left out.
Parker's sworn deposition says the British fired without provocation while Barker says the militia fired first: both given as accounts.

Left out: the Jonathan Harrington biography, the Oklahoma City bombing date, the National Guard units, the Boston Common anecdotes, the scalping rumour, the elderly militiamen who ambushed the ammunition convoy, and the article's own lines of poetry.
